overview.title: Running and checking an int8 matmul; model.quantize()
overview.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world
overview.section: 18.3 Speeding up training and inference with lower-precision computation
overview.main_topic: Finishing the hand-written abs-max quantizer, performing the int8 matmul, unscaling, comparing with the float32 result, and using Keras's built-in `model.quantize("int8")`.
overview.central_idea: The quantized matmul reproduces the float32 result to within about 0.02 while running the expensive part in int8; in practice you never write this by hand, because Keras's Dense, EinsumDense and Embedding layers implement it and `model.quantize("int8")` switches a whole model over.
overview.importance: It closes the loop on the quantization math with a concrete accuracy check and gives the one-line practical API.

Unscale an int8 matmul result with `x_scale * kernel_scale`.

prerequisites: The abs-max scheme and linearity argument (p.585).

summary:
The page finishes the function begun on p.585: after rounding and clipping, `abs_max_quantize` casts the scaled values to `int8` and returns both the integer tensor and its scale. It is applied to both operands: `int_x, x_scale = abs_max_quantize(x)` and `int_kernel, kernel_scale = abs_max_quantize(kernel)`.

Then comes the "faster" matmul and the unscaling: `int_y = ops.matmul(int_x, int_kernel)`, followed by `y = ops.cast(int_y, dtype="float32") / (x_scale * kernel_scale)`.

Comparing with the exact float32 product: the quantized `y` is `[[0.9843736, 0.3933239], [-1.0151455, -3.1965137]]`, while `ops.matmul(x, kernel)` gives `[[0.98, 0.40999997], [-1., -3.2]]`. "Pretty accurate!" The largest absolute error is about 0.017. For a large matmul this saves a lot of compute, since int8 computation can be considerably faster than even float16, and the only additions are fast elementwise ops: `abs`, `max`, `clip`, `cast`, `divide`, `multiply`.

The authors stress that you should not implement quantization by hand. Like float8, int8 quantization is built into the Keras `Dense`, `EinsumDense` and `Embedding` layers, which unlocks int8 inference for any Transformer-based model. Usage is three lines: instantiate a model (or any quantizable layer), call `model.quantize("int8")` ("Boom!"), and from then on `predict()` and `call()` run (partially) in int8.

paragraphs.excerpt: Now, of course, I don’t expect you to ever implement quantization by hand
paragraphs.what_it_says: Implementing quantization by hand would be impractical. As with float8, int8 quantization is built into Dense, EinsumDense and Embedding, enabling int8 inference for any Transformer-based model; the following code shows how to use it with any Keras model containing such layers.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Transformers are built almost entirely from these layers (projections, feedforward blocks, token embeddings), so quantizing them covers nearly all weights and FLOPs. Layers not on the list keep running in their usual dtype; hence 'partially' in the callout.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It turns the theory into a one-call deployment optimization, for example for the LLMs of chapter 16.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the Keras implementation quantizes kernels ahead of time (weights stored as int8 plus scales) and quantizes inputs on the fly at each call, which is the abs-max scheme applied per call, typically with finer-grained (per-channel/per-row) scales than the per-tensor example here.

concepts.name: int8 quantization
concepts.definition: Representing tensors as int8 values plus float scales so matmuls run in integer arithmetic.
concepts.intuition: Compute in a coarse integer unit, convert units once at the end.
concepts.significance: The page shows errors of about 0.02 on the toy example and a one-line Keras API.
concepts.misconception: Quantization is not lossless; the toy example shows small but nonzero errors.

concepts.name: Quantization error
concepts.definition: The difference between the quantized computation's output and the full-precision output, caused by rounding inputs to the integer grid.
concepts.intuition: Each input is off by at most half a grid step; dot products sum these small errors.
concepts.technical: For an entry $y_{ij}$ the error is roughly $\sum_k (\delta x_{ik} W_{kj} + x_{ik}\delta W_{kj})$ with $|\delta x| \le 0.5/s_x$, $|\delta W| \le 0.5/s_W$ (ignoring second-order terms).
concepts.significance: It bounds how much accuracy a quantized model can lose and shows that errors grow with the dot-product length unless they cancel.
concepts.misconception: Relative error is not uniform: outputs that are small due to cancellation suffer the most.

deeper.title: Why the 0.41 entry has the largest error
deeper.body: Entry (1,2) is $0.1\cdot(-2.2) + 0.9\cdot 0.7 = -0.22 + 0.63 = 0.41$. In integers: $11\cdot(-127) + 95\cdot 40 = -1397 + 3800 = 2403$. Exactly scaled, the two products would be $10.583\cdot(-127.0) \approx -1344$ and $95.25\cdot 40.41 \approx 3849$, summing to $\approx 2505$ (= $0.41 \times 6109.4$). Rounding 10.58 up to 11 makes the first product about 53 units more negative, and rounding 95.25 to 95 and 40.41 to 40 lowers the second by about 49 units: together about $-102$ units out of 2505, a relative error near 4%. Because the true result is the difference of two larger numbers, their absolute errors are large relative to the small result. Cancellation magnifies relative quantization error.

deeper.title: Cost accounting for a large matmul
deeper.body: For $X \in \mathbb{R}^{B\times d}$ and $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$: the matmul is $B d^2$ multiply-adds. Quantizing X needs $\approx 4Bd$ elementwise ops (abs, max, multiply, round/clip/cast), W can be quantized once ahead of time, and unscaling needs $Bd$ divides. With $d=4096$, overhead is roughly $5/4096 \approx 0.1\%$ of the matmul's operation count, so nearly all the int8 speedup is retained.

questions.question: Which elementwise ops does quantization add to the computation graph?
questions.answer: abs, max, clip, cast, divide, multiply.
questions.explanation: Listed on the page; they are cheap compared with the matmul.

questions.question: Why does the callout say predict() and call() run only 'partially' in int8 after model.quantize("int8")?
questions.answer: Only the quantizable layers (Dense, EinsumDense, Embedding) use int8; other operations such as normalization, activations and softmax still run in floating point, and inputs are dequantized after each int8 matmul.
questions.explanation: Follows from the restricted set of supported layers stated on the page.

questions.question: Why is quantization more worthwhile for a large matmul than for the 2x2 example?
questions.answer: The matmul cost grows as O(n^3) while the quantization overhead is elementwise, O(n^2); for large matrices the int8 speedup dominates.
questions.explanation: The page says that for a large matmul this saves a lot of compute, with only fast elementwise ops added.
